lesson_title: The Streetlight Nobody Would Pay For
hook_text: Nobody on your street would pay for the streetlight. So why is it on?
clip_script: Walk down your street and sort everything into two piles. The bread, the taxi, the airtime — you pay, you get. The market handles those. Now the streetlight. When it burns, it burns for EVERYONE — the woman on early shift, the shopkeeper, the learner at the taxi rank. Nobody can be fenced out of light. So ask: who volunteers to pay? Each neighbour thinks the same thing — if the others pay, I get it free; if they don't, my money is wasted. Everyone waits for everyone. The light stays off. Economists call it the free-rider problem, and it is why some things can ONLY be bought by all of us together, through tax. That's the public sector: the streetlight, the patrol, the drain, the road. But here's the twist the exam loves. Tax pays for it all — and tax has a breaking point. Tax the spaza at zero percent: government collects nothing. Tax it at a HUNDRED percent: the owner shuts the shop — government still collects nothing. Somewhere between sits the rate that collects the most, and past it, squeezing harder collects LESS. That hump has a name: the Laffer curve. The state needs your rand. It also needs to know when to stop asking.
visual_style: A dusk street scene where one streetlight flickers as neighbours peer from windows waiting for each other; the beam finally snaps on as coins flow into a shared pot, then the pot morphs into a rising-and-falling revenue hump over a spaza counter.
mood: Wry and thoughtful, ending on a clean punchline.
pacing: Patient through the waiting-neighbours standoff, a satisfying snap as the light comes on, brisk over the hump.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and take the free-rider, the budget and the Laffer curve into any Paper 1 essay.
